data.title: VW Mission Efficiency Deep Dive: Here’s how Volkswagen squeezed extraordinary EV range from just 54.9kWh
data.description:
Electric car makers have increasingly turned to bigger batteries to deliver longer driving ranges, but Volkswagen’s remarkable Mission Efficiency prototype demonstrates there’s another way.

The German brand’s ultra-slippery experimental EV has recorded average energy consumption of just 6.89kWh/100km during a 1278km European road trip, despite carrying a relatively modest 54.9kWh usable battery.

For some perspective, plenty of contemporary electric cars consume somewhere in the teens of kWh/100km, while larger and heavier electric SUVs can easily venture beyond 20kWh/100km.

READ MORE: 6.48kWh/100km! Volkswagen Mission Efficiency electric car shows how frugal an EV can be in the real world
READ MORE: Global unveiling: After many teases, the VW ID. Polo has been revealed in full. Is this the best small EV in the world?
READ MORE: Volkswagen turns iconic GTI on its head: Electric ID.3 is first rear-drive GTI and the most powerful ever

Volkswagen’s answer isn’t one breakthrough technology. Instead, it has attacked virtually everything that consumes or wastes energy, from aerodynamics and tyre resistance to braking, weight, climate control and even the stereo.

And much of what sits underneath the Mission Efficiency isn’t experimental.

Its 99kW front-mounted electric motor and battery are derived from the technology developed for the new Volkswagen ID. Polo, while the underlying front-wheel-drive MEB+ architecture will underpin a new generation of relatively affordable Volkswagen EVs.

That makes the Mission Efficiency an intriguing demonstration of how much further an EV might travel if engineers concentrate on reducing its energy requirement rather than simply adding more battery.

Aerodynamics

The Mission Efficiency’s most spectacular number is its drag coefficient of just 0.158.

But drag coefficient is only part of the equation. The VW also has a small frontal area of 2.08 square metres, helped by its unusually low 1392mm overall height.

Its body then progressively narrows towards the rear in the classic aerodynamic teardrop or ‘boat-tail’ shape.

Volkswagen has attacked the airflow in less obvious places too.

The underbody is almost completely enclosed, the rear wheels are covered and three active cooling flaps in the nose remain closed when cooling air isn’t required.

The doors use frameless windows and flush handles, while the rear axle has even been narrowed compared with the ID. Polo to help clean up airflow beneath the car.

The benefits increase dramatically with speed because aerodynamic drag becomes an increasingly important component of a vehicle’s total energy requirement.

Volkswagen claims the Mission Efficiency consumes more than 30 per cent less energy than an ID. Polo once speeds exceed 80km/h.

The most telling comparison comes at German autobahn speeds: VW says driving the Mission Efficiency at about 140km/h requires roughly the same amount of energy as driving an ID. Polo at 100km/h.

Wheels

One of the more fascinating lessons from the project concerns wheels.

Volkswagen estimates they are responsible for between 25 and 30 per cent of a vehicle’s aerodynamic resistance.

So rather than simply fitting conventional aero wheel covers, its engineers worked on controlling airflow both around and through them.

The front wheelarches sit closely around the tyres to reduce turbulence, while the rear wheels are completely enclosed.

VW has also developed patented deflectors mounted on the inside of all four wheels. Their job is to prevent air entering the rims and creating turbulence. Flat external wheel covers complete the package.

Then there are the tyres themselves. Volkswagen worked with Continental to develop special tyres based on its production EcoContact 7.

Their claimed rolling resistance is just 4.9kg per tonne, around 25 per cent below the threshold required to achieve the European Union’s highest Class A tyre rating.

Battery

Mission Efficiency’s battery is particularly interesting because its capacity is nothing extraordinary. It contains 54.9kWh of usable energy – less than many mainstream EVs.

It uses NMC lithium-ion chemistry and cell-to-pack construction, eliminating conventional intermediate battery modules by integrating cells more directly into the pack.

The battery is related to the production unit developed for the ID. Polo, although Volkswagen unlocked an additional 2.9kWh of usable capacity through software for Mission Efficiency.

Maximum DC charging power is 105kW and AC charging is rated at 11kW. Those aren’t headline-grabbing charging figures. The point is that Mission Efficiency needs relatively little electricity in the first place.

Its official WLTP energy consumption is just 8.4kWh/100km. During Volkswagen’s documented 1278.36km journey from Wolfsburg in Germany to Vienna in Austria, that fell to 6.89kWh/100km excluding charging losses, or 7.51kWh/100km when those losses were included.

The battery required only one recharge during the journey and VW says the car arrived with another 164km of indicated range remaining.

A separate idealised test at a constant 68km/h, without gradients and with energy consumers such as air-conditioning switched off, produced an even lower 6.48kWh/100km.

Braking

Another potential pointer towards future production EVs is hidden in the braking system.

Mission Efficiency retains conventional hydraulic brakes at the front but uses a new electromechanical brake at the rear, developed jointly by Volkswagen and automotive technology company Aumovio.

Rather than hydraulic pressure activating the rear brakes, electrical actuators do the job. That eliminates rear hydraulic lines and brake fluid while reducing mechanical friction losses.

More importantly for an EV, Volkswagen says the system enables variable brake-force distribution and can improve the interaction between friction braking and regenerative braking.

That potentially allows more of the vehicle’s kinetic energy to be recovered and returned to the battery rather than disappearing as heat through the brakes.

Solar

There is also a 370-watt photovoltaic system integrated into the glass roof and rear section of the Mission Efficiency.

Volkswagen says it can contribute the equivalent of up to 30km of extra range per day, depending heavily on location, weather and season.

But that needs some qualification. The solar cells aren’t intended to transform Mission Efficiency into a solar-powered EV. They feed the vehicle’s electrical system and reduce the amount of energy ancillary systems need to draw from the traction battery.

It’s another example of the philosophy behind the entire car: rather than finding one enormous energy saving, VW has accumulated lots of smaller ones.

Air-conditioning

Climate control can take a significant bite out of an EV’s available energy, particularly when heating the cabin in cold conditions.

Mission Efficiency therefore uses a heat pump to reduce the electrical energy required for heating. The system uses R744 – carbon dioxide – as its refrigerant rather than a conventional synthetic refrigerant.

Volkswagen has applied the same energy-saving philosophy elsewhere inside. There’s no conventional infotainment screen. Instead, occupants bring a smartphone or tablet.

Even conventional permanently installed speakers have been deleted and replaced by a portable Bluetooth speaker.

Weight

The Mission Efficiency combines elements of the ID. Polo structure with a self-supporting aluminium construction, while the doors, bonnet, tailgate, guards and other components employ carbon-fibre and aramid composite materials.

That part of the formula is clearly less representative of an affordable production EV than its motor and battery technology, because extensive lightweight composites remain expensive.

Nevertheless, it illustrates the engineering trade-off inherent in long-range EVs.

Adding battery capacity increases range, but also adds weight. That additional weight then requires more energy to accelerate and move, potentially requiring still more battery capacity.

Mission Efficiency attacks the problem from the opposite direction.

Mirrors

There’s even an interesting lesson in something Volkswagen decided not to fit.

Despite the extreme aerodynamic focus, Mission Efficiency retains conventional exterior mirrors rather than replacing them with cameras.

Volkswagen says wind-tunnel development showed the overall aerodynamic benefit from camera mirrors would have been relatively small.

They would also have added cost and consumed electricity.

It’s a tiny detail, but one that neatly sums up the project: a technology doesn’t automatically make the car more efficient simply because it looks more advanced.

What are the implications for future VW EVs?

Don’t expect an ID. Polo with covered rear wheels, carbon-fibre body panels and a Cd of 0.158. Mission Efficiency is a technology demonstrator rather than a preview of a production model.

But its significance is that the fundamental electrical hardware isn’t exotic.

The 99kW APP290 permanent-magnet motor, battery technology and front-wheel-drive MEB+ architecture have strong links with Volkswagen’s new generation of production EVs.

Other technologies – active cooling flaps, improved underbody aerodynamics, lower-resistance tyres, smarter thermal management, reduced brake drag and better wheel aerodynamics – are far more transferable to everyday cars than Mission Efficiency’s dramatic body shape suggests.

And that’s perhaps the most important lesson from the project. The industry’s EV range battle has often focused on how many kilowatt-hours can be squeezed beneath a vehicle.

Mission Efficiency demonstrates the other side of the equation. Make an electric car require substantially fewer kilowatt-hours to travel each 100km and suddenly a relatively modest battery can take you a very long way.

The post VW Mission Efficiency Deep Dive: Here’s how Volkswagen squeezed extraordinary EV range from just 54.9kWh appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Fastest Mitsubishi yet: 342kW ASX VR-e electric SUV confirmed for Australia, with starting price expected in the $40,000s
data.description:
Mitsubishi has confirmed its new ASX VR-e electric SUV will offer up to 342kW and a claimed 3.9-second 0-100km/h sprint when it arrives in Australian showrooms in late 2026.

The dual-motor, all-wheel drive GSR will head a four-model range and, according to Mitsubishi, become the fastest-accelerating vehicle the Japanese brand has officially sold in Australia.

EV Central understands the ASX VR-e range will start somewhere in the $40,000s before on-road costs, positioning the Kia EV3 – which starts at $47,600 – as a logical rival on price.

READ MORE: The wait is over! Reborn Mitsubishi Pajero finally revealed – but where is the PHEV?
READ MORE: Mitsubishi ASX VR-e EV confirmed for Australia: Foxconn-built electric SUV gets famous badge, local tuning and Q4 2026 launch
READ MORE: Mitsubishi reveals shock new EV! Eclipse name returns on SUV developed with Nissan

Mitsubishi has yet to announce exact pricing or Australian driving range figures ahead of the small electric SUV’s late-2026 launch.

The latest specifications confirm the first EV offered by Mitsubishi Australia since the i-Miev will come in rear-wheel drive LS, Aspire and Exceed grades, topped by the all-wheel drive GSR.

All four use a 57.7kWh lithium iron phosphate battery. The rear-drive versions produce 171kW and 350Nm and are claimed to reach 100km/h in 6.8 seconds.

Adding a second motor to the front axle lifts the GSR’s combined outputs to 342kW and 700Nm.

Mitsubishi has yet to announce Australian driving range figures. However, the related Foxtron Bria sold in Taiwan claims 516km for its rear-drive versions and 466km for its all-wheel drive flagship under the more lenient NEDC test cycle.

An interior photograph supplied by Mitsubishi also shows an indicated 175km remaining at 47 per cent battery charge, equivalent to roughly 372km at a full charge. However, this is a dashboard estimate rather than an official tested range, and the variant pictured has not been identified.

As previously reported, the Taiwanese-built ASX VR-e is sourced through Foxconn’s automotive business Foxtron and is related to the Pininfarina-designed Bria. It is separate from the Renault Captur-based petrol ASX introduced locally in 2025.

Mitsubishi has also previously confirmed Australian testing and tuning for the new EV, along with its own styling treatment. The VR-e name references the Galant VR-4 that preceded the Lancer Evolution in the brand’s performance line-up.

The ASX VR-e measures 4315mm long, 1885mm wide and 1535mm tall, with a 2800mm wheelbase, giving it the proportions of a low-slung small SUV.

Its aerodynamic features include an S-Duct that channels air through the front bumper and over the bonnet, along with air curtains, active grille shutters and flush-fitting door handles.

DC fast charging peaks at 134kW across the range, while AC charging is limited to 6.6kW. Mitsubishi has not supplied charging times in the latest announcement.

Vehicle-to-load capability is standard, allowing the battery to power external electrical equipment through the charging port, although its output has not been detailed.

Drivers can choose from five regenerative braking settings, including a full one-pedal driving mode, as well as Eco, Comfort and Sport drive modes and three steering assistance settings.

In the GSR, Sport mode changes the nominal front-to-rear power split from 50:50 to 30:70, except under full throttle.

Inside, every grade gets a 15.6-inch central touchscreen, a 9.2-inch digital instrument display and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

Despite the touchscreen’s role in controlling vehicle functions, Mitsubishi has retained physical switches for key climate functions, the hazard lights and front and rear demisters. A customisable favourites switch is also included.

The system supports over-the-air updates, with connected services available from launch.

The entry-level LS comes with 18-inch alloy wheels, cloth upholstery, manually adjustable front seats, dual-zone climate control, a six-speaker audio system and a reversing camera.

The rear seat has a 60:40 split-fold arrangement and a separate load-through opening.

Stepping up to Aspire adds synthetic leather upholstery, power-adjustable heated and ventilated front seats, driver’s seat memory, 64-colour ambient lighting and automatically operating flush door handles.

It also gains a front storage compartment with an electric bonnet release, an adjustable rear cargo floor, adaptive driving beam headlights, a 360-degree camera and parking assistance, including a straight-line remote parking function.

The Exceed adds 20-inch alloy wheels, a panoramic glass roof, a hands-free powered tailgate and a 12-speaker SEAS audio system.

Along with its second motor and all-wheel drive, the GSR gets synthetic leather and microsuede upholstery with blue stitching, plus a black-roof exterior finish.

The driver assistance package includes autonomous emergency braking, adaptive cruise control with lane following, lane keeping assistance, blind spot detection, rear cross traffic alert, traffic sign recognition and driver monitoring.

Mitsubishi has also detailed separate vehicle and battery warranty arrangements.

The drive battery is covered for eight years or 160,000km against material and manufacturing defects, with a capacity care program providing protection for at least 70 per cent of its usable energy capacity over that period.

The vehicle is eligible for Mitsubishi’s 10-year/200,000km warranty when scheduled servicing is completed within the required intervals at its dealerships. Otherwise, a five-year/100,000km vehicle warranty applies.

Capped-price servicing covers the first 10 scheduled services, up to 10 years or 150,000km, with service intervals of 12 months or 15,000km. Roadside assistance can also be extended annually through eligible servicing for up to 10 years.

Mitsubishi ASX VR-e: Grade walk

The ASX VR-e starts with the LS grade, which features the following:

  • Single-motor, rear-wheel drive
  • 18” alloy wheels
  • 5-stage regenerative braking adjustment (including full single pedal mode
  • Flush door handles – manual operation
  • Black/grey cloth seat trim
  • 6-way driver seat manual adjustment
  • 4-way passenger seat manual adjustment
  • 2nd row 60/40 split fold flat
  • 2nd row load through (ski hatch)
  • Rear park assist – 2 x parking sensor
  • Rear view monitor
  • Dual-zone Climate Control
  • 6-speaker audio
  • 57.7 kWh Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) battery
  • ECO/Comfort/Sport Drive modes
  • CCS2 DC Charging – maximum 134 kW
  • Type 2 AC Charging – maximum 6.6 kW
  • Vehicle to Load (V2L) via external Type 2 AC charging port
  • Proximity door lock/unlock
  • LED headlights with Auto High Beam (AHB)
  • LED daytime running lamps
  • LED taillights
  • 9.2” Digital Driver Display
  • 15.6” Infotainment touchscreen
    • Wireless CarPlay and Android Auto connectivity
  • Driver Monitoring System (DMS)

ASPIRE models retain the above, plus:

  • Flush door handles – automatic operation
  • D-pillar trims with etched finish
  • Black Artificial Leather seat trim
  • 8-way driver seat power adjustment
  • Driver seat memory
  • Driver seat heating and cooling
  • 4-way passenger seat power adjustment
  • Passenger seat heating and cooling
  • 64-colour selectable interior ambient lighting
  • Frunk with electric bonnet release
  • Adjustable height rear cargo floor
  • Adaptive Driving Beam
  • Front park assist – 6 x parking sensor
  • Rear park assist – 6 x parking sensor
  • Surround view monitor with 360 o camera
  • Autonomous parking

EXCEED models retain the above, plus:

  • 20” two-tone alloy wheels
  • Panoramic glass roof
  • Electric tailgate with hands-free operation
  • 12-speaker SEAS sound system

GSR models retain the above, plus:

  • Dual motor All-Wheel Drive system
  • Black Artificial Leather (PU+PVC) with microsuede seat trim
  • Blue stitching on seats
  • Two-tone exterior paint finish

The post Fastest Mitsubishi yet: 342kW ASX VR-e electric SUV confirmed for Australia, with starting price expected in the $40,000s appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Confirmed for Australia in mid-2027: New Hyundai Tucson goes all-hybrid to rival Toyota RAV4 and an increasing number of Chinese rivals
data.description:
Hyundai’s new-generation Tucson will arrive in Australia in mid-2027 with an exclusively hybrid launch line-up, as the Korean brand prepares to take on the Toyota RAV4 and an expanding wave of electrified Chinese competitors.

The fifth-generation of one of Australia’s most popular medium SUVs will also introduce a rugged-looking XRT variant locally, although the more capable XRT Pro and the plug-in hybrid offered overseas are not part of the Australian launch plans.

The Australian launch timing has been confirmed alongside the Tucson’s global unveiling in New York, following its initial appearance in South Korea in August.

READ MORE: Another electric van enters the fray: Hyundai Staria Load Electric lands at $70,990 with 450km range and ultra-fast charging
READ MORE: Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program
READ MORE: Revealed: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute tech will debut in Santa Fe SUV range extender

Pricing for the new Tucson has yet to be announced. The current Australian range starts at $40,100 before on-road costs for the petrol front-wheel drive model, with the hybrid starting at $42,850.

The fifth-generation family SUV brings a larger body, a redesigned cabin and Hyundai’s next-generation hybrid technology.

The Tucson’s increased emphasis on electrification comes as Chinese brands broaden the choices available to Australian family SUV buyers.

Alongside its established Toyota RAV4 rival, the Hyundai will compete with vehicles such as the BYD Sealion 6, GWM Haval H6 and Chery Tiggo 7 Super Hybrid, which have brought plug-in hybrid power into the mainstream medium SUV market.

At the centre of the new Tucson’s electrification push is a revised hybrid system combining a 1.6-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine with a new transmission incorporating two electric motors.

Overseas specifications put combined output at 174–180kW and 380Nm, compared with 172kW and 367Nm for the outgoing Australian Tucson Hybrid. The new system uses a six-speed automatic transmission and a 1.49kWh battery, with front- and all-wheel drive versions available. Final Australian specifications remain unconfirmed.

Hyundai’s new hybrid architecture adds a motor that handles engine starting and electricity generation, while the main drive motor provides propulsion and regenerative braking. Hyundai says the arrangement improves efficiency and refinement, with smoother shifts and reduced noise and vibration.

The new Tucson Hybrid also introduces an E-Traction function that manages driving torque to reduce wheel slip during cornering.

A Stay Mode allows occupants to use functions including air-conditioning, audio and device charging with the engine switched off while parked. Hyundai has not specified how long the Tucson can maintain those functions before the engine needs to restart.

Globally, the new plug-in hybrid pairs a 1.6-litre turbo-petrol engine with electric propulsion for a combined 215kW and approximately 380Nm.

Hyundai estimates an electric driving range of 81km, although the release does not identify the test cycle or battery capacity. A 7.2kW onboard AC charger is also specified.

A conventional 1.6-litre turbo-petrol engine with an eight-speed automatic remains part of the global line-up.

The new model also grows substantially. Australia gets the long-wheelbase version, measuring 4700mm long, 1905mm wide and 1685mm high. A short-wheelbase version is built for Europe.overseas

That makes it 60mm longer, 40mm wider and 20mm taller than its predecessor, providing more cabin space beneath the more upright and angular bodywork.

Its styling replaces the current Tucson’s intricate grille and sharply creased flanks with squared-off proportions, prominent wheelarches and a horizontal lighting theme framed by vertical lamps.

Rear doors now open to 83 degrees, compared with 73 degrees previously, to improve access.

Inside, Hyundai has separated the driver display from the central touchscreen, replacing the current model’s paired-screen layout with a slim 9.9-inch instrument display and either a 12.9-inch or 17-inch infotainment screen, depending on specification.

Physical buttons remain for frequently used climate and audio functions, while the gear selector is mounted on the steering column.

Available equipment includes two 15W wireless phone chargers. However, three-zone climate control, front-seat massage and reclining relaxation seats are reserved for the short-wheelbase version Australia will not receive.

The Tucson also adopts Hyundai’s Pleos Connect infotainment system, based on Android Automotive, with over-the-air updates, downloadable applications and a conversational AI assistant called Gleo.

Beyond the road-focused versions, Hyundai has expanded the Tucson’s adventure offering with an XRT Pro that adds hardware upgrades to the tougher styling of the regular XRT.

The XRT Pro has all-wheel drive, all-terrain tyres, front recovery hooks and 210mm ground clearance — 30mm more than the standard model — along with revised approach and departure angles.

The XRT Pro also introduces Smart Terrain Assist, which assesses traction and wheel slip, and a low-speed control system that manages acceleration and braking between 2km/h and 25km/h.

Depending on market and specification, the Tucson also offers a camera view of the ground beneath the vehicle, assistance for reversing along a previously driven route and trailer reversing assistance.

Hyundai has announced improved towing capability overseas, but Australian towing limits remain unconfirmed.

A further sport-themed Tucson variant will be unveiled at the Paris motor show on October 12.

According to August year-to-date VFACTS figures, Hyundai sold 14,272 Tucsons in the first eight months of 2026, up 5.5 per cent on the same period last year. That placed it fourth among Australia’s best-selling medium SUVs behind the Tesla Model Y (31,454), Toyota RAV4 (26,585) and BYD Sealion 7 (17,277).

The post Confirmed for Australia in mid-2027: New Hyundai Tucson goes all-hybrid to rival Toyota RAV4 and an increasing number of Chinese rivals appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Another Chinese people-mover is eyeing Australia: LDV MIFA 7 EV under evaluation as MPV battle explodes
data.description:
Australia’s rapidly expanding field of Chinese electrified people-movers could be about to get another entrant, with the LDV Mifa 7 electric MPV under evaluation for local sale.

The seven-seat battery-electric Mifa 7 has appeared again in Australian Government homologation document after first appearing in 2024.

It is understood LDV’s Australian distributor Ateco Automotive is currently evaluating the Mifa 7 for local sale.

READ MORE: LDV extends Australia’s cheapest electric van at $47,990 as eDeliver 7 gets huge $9000 discount
READ MORE: LDV eT60 electric ute, eDeliver 9 van and MIFA 9 people mover have big EV price premiums
READ MORE: Futuristic, hyper-fast LDV electric people-mover possible for Australia

The development comes as what was once one of the quieter corners of the Australian new-car market attracts an extraordinary influx of Chinese brands and electrified models.

The GAC M8 plug-in hybrid, battery-electric Zeekr 009, Denza D9 and XPeng X9 are here or coming. BYD’s M9 plug-in hybrid is joining the battle, while GWM’s new Wey premium brand has gained Australian approval for hybrid and PHEV versions of its G9.

New Chinese brand Forthing has confirmed an electric and plug-in hybrid people-mover for the first half of 2027.

Beyond China, Korea’s Kia is getting in on the action too, with the battery-electric seven-seat PV5 Passenger due to join the Australian market.

The MIFA 7 is produced by SAIC Maxus, the Chinese arm of state-owned SAIC Motor whose vehicles are sold under the LDV badge in Australia. In its home market the people-mover is now known as the Maxus Dajia 7, while MIFA 7 is used in export markets and is the name listed on its Australian homologation documents.

At 4907mm long, 1885mm wide and 1756mm high, with a 2975mm wheelbase, it is significantly more compact than the large luxury-focused electric MPVs that have led the Chinese charge. Those dimensions are confirmed by the Australian approval documentation.

By comparison, the Denza D9 stretches to 5250mm and the BYD M9 plug-in hybrid is 5145mm long.

The MIFA 7 is also substantially smaller than LDV’s own MIFA 9, which pioneered the battery-electric people-mover segment in Australia when it launched in 2022.

The MIFA 9 is no longer part of LDV’s active Australian model range. LDV paused sales of both the petrol MIFA and electric MIFA 9 late last year as it monitored the people-mover market, although it stopped short of formally discontinuing either model.

The smaller MIFA 7 could potentially give LDV another way into a segment that has changed dramatically since the MIFA 9 arrived.

The latest Australian Road Vehicle Descriptor lists two MIFA 7 variants, both configured with seven seats and a single 180kW electric motor. Battery capacities are 77kWh and 90kWh.

The government documentation doesn’t specify driving range, but overseas versions provide a useful guide. In Hong Kong the 77kWh MIFA 7 is rated at 410km WLTP and the 90kWh version at 480km WLTP, with the electric motor producing 180kW and 350Nm.

Both Australian-approved variants have a 1500kg braked towing capacity, while tare weight is listed at 2159kg for the 77kWh model and 2239kg for the 90kWh version.

In China, a plug-in hybrid powertrain is alo offered.

Australian approval documents for the model first emerged in 2024, when it appeared likely to become LDV’s second electric people-mover, but the vehicle never progressed to a local launch.

The Mifa 7 has been on sale in the right-hand drive UK market since 2024.

The post Another Chinese people-mover is eyeing Australia: LDV MIFA 7 EV under evaluation as MPV battle explodes appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Revealed! How Chery SUV brand Freelander will take the fight to BYD Denza in Australia in 2027
data.description:
The Freelander 8 electrified SUV will arrive in Australia in 2027, with the Chery-JLR joint venture firming up its local launch plans and outlining seating options, dealer support and the management team behind the new brand.

Freelander will join Chery, Omoda, Jaecoo, Lepas and iCaur in Australia udner the Chery unbrella. Another Chery brand, Jetour, is set to be sold separately in Australia.

Measuring more than 5.1 metres long, the Chinese-built SUV will lead Freelander’s Australian introduction, targeting buyers in the premium large SUV market.

READ MORE: Freelander 8: More details revealed about Aussie-bound Chery-JLR co-developed electrified SUV aimed at BMW iX3 and Denza B5
READ MORE: Confirmed: Electrified Freelander 8 locked and loaded for Australia. Coming to fight Denza B5, Toyota Prado and Ford Everest
READ MORE: Land Rover Freelander is back! JLR and China’s Chery reinvent mid-size 4WD as a cool, blocky all-electric SUV to fight inbound battery-powered Toyota LandCruiser

The latest announcement confirms five- and six-seat configurations for the Freelander 8, although Australian specifications, pricing and a more precise launch date remain undisclosed.

Australia and New Zealand have been identified as priority right-hand-drive markets, with both scheduled to launch Freelander next year.

The announcement follows confirmation in May that Freelander would come to Australia with an independent dealer network. At that stage, no firm local launch timing had been provided.

Freelander Australia and New Zealand will be headed by Kym Mellow, whose previous automotive industry roles include positions with Inchcape Australasia and Mazda Australia.

His responsibilities cover the brand’s establishment, product planning, sales, marketing, aftersales and dealer network development. Recruitment for other senior leadership positions is underway.

Freelander says it will work with established local dealerships, with sales and service coverage planned for metropolitan and selected regional areas.

Dealer appointments will be announced before launch, with the company promising trained sales and service staff, parts support and dedicated showroom facilities.

The new operation revives a name previously used by Land Rover, but Freelander is now a standalone brand produced by Chery Jaguar Land Rover, the Chinese companies’ 50:50 joint venture.

JLR licensed the Freelander name to the joint venture in June 2024. JLR leads design, while Chery contributes electrified powertrain technology, engineering and supply-chain resources.

Production takes place at the joint venture’s Changshu factory in Jiangsu Province, which has also built the Land Rover Discovery Sport and Range Rover Evoque.

The first Freelander 8 rolled off the production line on July 30, 2026.

Earlier disclosures outlined battery-electric and range-extender powertrains for the Freelander range, but the Australian announcement does not identify which versions will be sold here.

A range-extender uses a combustion engine to generate electricity for an electrically driven vehicle, providing additional driving range beyond that available from its rechargeable battery.

Previously revealed Freelander 8 technology includes an 800-volt electrical architecture, CATL battery technology, height-adjustable dual-chamber air suspension and nine driving modes.

Cabin details disclosed in July included a 15.6-inch central touchscreen and a 47.2-inch panoramic display beneath the windscreen, along with physical controls and dual wireless phone chargers. Australian availability of that equipment remains to be confirmed.

The SUV’s size and positioning put it in contention for buyers considering premium family SUVs, while its intended all-terrain capability also brings electrified off-roaders such as the Denza B5 into the frame. Pricing and local powertrain choices will determine its closest competitors.

Freelander’s Australian plans form part of a broader international expansion following its Chinese launch on September 3. The United Arab Emirates is its first overseas market, with an international brand launch held in Abu Dhabi on September 29.

According to Freelander, the 8 attracted more than 10,000 pre-orders in China within 48 hours of orders opening.

The brand plans to introduce six models over the next five years, although it has not detailed which subsequent vehicles will come to Australia.

The post Revealed! How Chery SUV brand Freelander will take the fight to BYD Denza in Australia in 2027 appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Tesla Model 3 drops below $46,000! New entry grade undercuts BYD Seal as well as Kia EV4
data.description:
Tesla has lowered the Australian entry price of its Model 3 to $45,900 before on-road costs with a new Rear-Wheel Drive grade that brings the electric sedan into closer competition with Australia’s biggest selling sedan, the Toyota Camry hybrid.

The new variant is $9000 cheaper than the continuing $54,900 Model 3 Premium Rear-Wheel Drive, a reduction of about 16.4 per cent in the range’s starting price.

Orders open today (October 1), with Australian customer deliveries scheduled to begin in mid-to-late October. Showroom displays and test drives are due to commence during the same period.

READ MORE:
READ MORE:
READ MORE:

The move puts the Model 3 below the $46,990 BYD Seal Dynamic and $4090 below the $49,990 Kia EV4 Air Standard Range. Mazda’s Chinese-built 6e liftback also starts at $49,990 before on-road costs.

It positions the new Tesla as Australia’s cheapest battery electric sedan on those advertised base prices, although the final drive-away comparison will depend on on-road charges and any rival offers.

The price also narrows the gap to the Toyota Camry Ascent hybrid, which starts at $39,990 before on-road costs. The new Model 3 carries a $5910 premium over the Toyota, compared with $14,910 for the Premium RWD.

The new entry model Tesla combines woven textile and synthetic leather seat trim with heated, electrically adjustable front seats. Tesla explicitly confirms the rear passenger touchscreen has been deleted, although rear air vents and two USB-C charging ports remain.

A 16-inch central touchscreen, seven-speaker audio system, wireless phone charging and footwell ambient lighting are included.

Other standard equipment includes a panoramic glass roof, 18-inch Prismata wheels, matrix LED headlights, power-folding exterior mirrors, a powered boot lid, heated steering wheel and heat pump.

Tesla claims up to 572km of WLTP driving range and a 0–100km/h acceleration time of 6.2 seconds.

The company says the existing battery pack carries over, but its announcement does not specify battery capacity, motor output or AC and DC charging rates.

Combined boot and under-bonnet storage is quoted at 682 litres, increasing to 1659 litres with the rear seats folded.

The new RWD also supports Tesla’s Power Share function, allowing the traction battery to supply electricity to appliances and devices through a separately purchased Tesla Outlet Adapter.

Connected features include phone-key access, remote cabin pre-conditioning, charging schedules, over-the-air software updates and access to Tesla’s Supercharger network.

Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software is available as an optional $149 monthly subscription. Despite its name, the system requires driver supervision.

The lower-priced variant expands the Australian Model 3 range to four grades. Above it sit the Premium Rear-Wheel Drive at $54,900, Premium Long-Range Rear-Wheel Drive at $61,900 and Performance All-Wheel Drive at $80,900, all before on-road costs.

The pricing change arrives as competition for electrified passenger-car buyers broadens beyond the established Model 3 and BYD Seal.

Alongside the Kia EV4 and Mazda 6e, BYD’s Seal 6 plug-in hybrid sedan starts at $34,990 before on-road costs. Although it uses a different powertrain, it gives buyers another lower-priced alternative to both the Tesla and Camry.

Zeekr’s forthcoming 7GT electric wagon will add another option for buyers seeking an alternative to an SUV. Its Australian launch is scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026, with initial deliveries in the first quarter of 2027; local pricing remains unannounced.

The Camry remains the larger seller across the year, although the Model 3 moved ahead in August.

Electric Vehicle Council figures show 1271 Model 3 deliveries in August, while VFACTS recorded 967 Camrys. Across the first eight months of 2026, the Model 3 recorded 4597 deliveries compared with 8405 for the Camry. Tesla reports through the Electric Vehicle Council rather than VFACTS.

The BYD Seal recorded 433 deliveries in August and 3481 for the year to date, placing it behind the Model 3 on both measures.

The new Tesla carries a five-year, unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty and eight-year/160,000km battery and drive-unit coverage, with a minimum 70 per cent battery-capacity retention guarantee.

data.title: Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program
data.description:
Hyundai is preparing a new generation of cheaper, faster-charging and longer-lasting batteries to underpin a massive global product offensive that will see more than 100 new or updated vehicles launched by the end of the decade.

The Korean auto giant has detailed an extensive battery development program that includes new in-house battery cells, a switch to significantly cheaper mid-nickel chemistry for upcoming EVs, smarter battery management and new technology designed to prevent thermal runaway spreading through a battery pack.

It comes as Hyundai prepares one of the largest product rollouts in its history, with more than 100 global launches and major model updates planned by 2030.

READ MORE: Revealed: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute tech will debut in Santa Fe SUV range extender
READ MORE: Hyundai Ioniq 3 priced: UK version of new EV rival for BYD and MG starts at $42,500 … that’s promising for Australia
READ MORE: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute delayed: It’s still coming to Australia but it could take until 2030 to get here

More than 18 will take Hyundai into new products or market segments and seven new vehicles are due within the next eight months alone.

The rollout will include conventional combustion-powered vehicles, hybrids, extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) and battery-electric vehicles, with electrified models targeted to account for 60 per cent of Hyundai sales by 2030, up from 23 per cent in 2025.

Hyundai is targeting 5.55 million global vehicle sales and a six per cent global market share by the end of the decade.

Central to the technology push is Hyundai’s development of its own battery cells.

The company claims its new high-performance cells can produce more than twice the output of the high-nickel cells it has previously used while reducing charging time by 40 per cent.

The first application will be Hyundai’s new EREV powertrain arriving in the first half of 2027.

That system will initially appear in the new Santa Fe EREV, which Hyundai says will offer more than 600 miles – about 965km – of total driving range.

Hyundai says the EREV requires less than half the battery capacity of a comparable battery-electric vehicle while still providing equivalent battery performance and EV driving characteristics.

The technology is also significant for Australia because EREV is emerging as a leading candidate to power Hyundai’s upcoming body-on-frame midsize ute.

But Hyundai’s battery plans extend well beyond EREVs.

One of the biggest developments for conventional battery-electric vehicles will arrive from 2027.

Hyundai says EVs launching next year will adopt mid-nickel NCM – nickel-cobalt-manganese – battery cells that will reduce battery costs by around 30 per cent compared with the technology they replace.

Importantly, Hyundai claims the cheaper cells will maintain what it describes as “optimal performance” under real-world driving conditions.

The potential significance is substantial because the battery remains one of the most expensive individual components in an electric vehicle.

A 30 per cent reduction in battery cost does not mean the price of an entire Hyundai EV will fall by 30 per cent, but reducing the cost of the pack potentially gives the company much greater scope to lower vehicle prices – or fit larger batteries and more equipment without pushing prices higher.

It should also help Hyundai compete against the rapidly expanding number of lower-cost Chinese EV manufacturers.

The first models using the new mid-nickel batteries have not been identified.

However, they will arrive during an enormous expansion of Hyundai’s electrified range.

In Europe alone Hyundai plans to cover 85 per cent of the market with a fully electrified portfolio, including five new SUVs and light-commercial vehicles, while increasing annual EV sales from 116,000 in 2025 to more than 420,000 by 2030.

Hyundai isn’t concentrating purely on the chemistry inside the battery.

Software will increasingly be used to manage the battery throughout its working life.

Hyundai says an enhanced cloud-based battery management system (BMS) will extend the average life of its EV batteries by 20 per cent by 2028.

The system will monitor battery condition and use cloud connectivity to detect abnormalities in individual cells in real time.

That could have implications beyond how long owners can keep their cars.

Battery degradation and the cost of replacing an EV battery remain important considerations for used EV buyers, while improved battery longevity potentially increases residual values and extends the useful life of an electric vehicle.

Hyundai hasn’t detailed exactly how it has calculated its claimed 20 per cent average battery-life improvement or translated it into expected kilometres or years of service.

The other major component of Hyundai’s battery strategy is safety.

Hyundai has developed what it calls Thermal Runaway Protection (TRP), designed to prevent heat from a failing battery cell spreading into adjacent cells.

Thermal runaway occurs when a battery cell experiences an uncontrolled increase in temperature that can trigger further cells, potentially creating a chain reaction within the battery pack.

Rather than simply delaying the spread of heat, Hyundai claims its TRP system can block it at the source.

It combines a battery design that dissipates heat with barriers between individual cells intended to stop heat transfer.

Hyundai says the technology has been verified through more than 200 repeated tests using both prismatic and pouch-type NCM batteries.

The cloud-based BMS and TRP effectively provide two layers of defence.

The BMS is intended to detect abnormal behaviour early enough for preventative action to be taken, while TRP provides a physical defence against heat spreading if a cell does fail.

The new thermal-runaway technology will make its production debut with Genesis, with Hyundai’s roadmap identifying the upcoming electric GV90 flagship SUV as its first application.

The battery investment is part of a broader change in Hyundai’s electrification strategy.

Rather than relying exclusively on battery-electric vehicles, Hyundai is expanding across EVs, hybrids and EREVs as it pushes towards its 5.55-million annual sales target.

Among the models identified in the latest roadmap are the IONIQ 3, new-generation Tucson and Tucson Hybrid, Santa Fe EREV, a new electric SUV for India and new global and European B-segment SUVs.

Genesis will simultaneously expand beyond pure EVs with its first hybrid, the GV80 Hybrid, as well as an EREV SUV targeting more than 640 miles – around 1030km – of total range and the battery-electric GV90 flagship.

The post Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Cheaper Toyota RAV4 PHEV confirmed for 2027: New GXL will bring price closer to Chinese SUV rivals
data.description:
Toyota will lower the entry price of its RAV4 plug-in hybrid range in early 2027, adding a GXL front-wheel-drive model as competition from Chinese-built electrified SUVs continues to expand.

The RAV4 GXL 2WD PHEV will arrive in the first quarter of 2027, joining the existing XSE front- and all-wheel-drive versions and flagship GR Sport AWD. Toyota has yet to announce its price.

READ MORE: 2026 Toyota RAV4 PHEV Review: New plug-in hybrid takes the fight to GWM, Haval, BYD
READ MORE: New 2026 Toyota RAV4 could make history as Australia’s first electrified and SUV top-seller
READ MORE: 2026 Toyota RAV4 Aussie range detailed: PHEV and hybrid on the way, but so are price rises

However, the current RAV4 pricing structure suggests a starting point around $53,000–$54,000 before on-road costs, potentially lowering the price of entry by about $5000–$6000.

The clearest comparison is between the existing XSE AWD hybrid and plug-in hybrid. The ordinary hybrid costs $58,340, while the PHEV is $63,340 — a $5000 premium. Applying that same premium to the $48,990 GXL front-wheel-drive hybrid produces an estimated price of $53,990. These are calculations based on existing prices, rather than Toyota guidance.

There is also an argument for a slightly lower figure. Toyota charges $3350 to move from front- to all-wheel drive in its GX, GXL and Cruiser hybrids, compared with $4500 between the two XSE PHEVs.

Allowing for that difference implies a front-wheel-drive plug-in premium of $3850, which would put the GXL PHEV at $52,840. Final pricing will depend on Toyota’s positioning and any changes to the range before its arrival.

Either estimate would bring the Toyota closer to an increasingly crowded field of Chinese plug-in hybrid SUVs, although several rivals would retain a substantial price advantage.

Current alternatives include the Geely Starray EM-i from $37,490 before on-road costs, Chery Tiggo 7 PHEV from $39,990 drive-away, Jaecoo J7 PHEV from $43,990 drive-away and GWM Haval H6 PHEV from $47,990 drive-away.

GWM is also preparing to launch its new Haval H7 PHEV in October, with an indicated price between $50,000 and $60,000. Its 320kW all-wheel-drive powertrain will offer considerably more power than the front-wheel-drive Toyota.

Further competition will arrive in the second half of 2027 with Ford’s Chinese-developed and built Bronco Basecamp.

The Ford uses a range-extender powertrain, with electric motors driving the wheels and a petrol engine generating electricity. Australian pricing remains unannounced, although an anticipated starting point around $55,000 would put it close to the cheaper RAV4 PHEV if both estimates prove accurate.

The new GXL will retain a substantial equipment list, including 18-inch alloy wheels, LED lighting, an eight-way powered driver’s seat, dual-zone climate control, keyless entry and start, rain-sensing wipers and wireless phone charging.

A 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster and 10.5-inch multimedia touchscreen are also included, along with synthetic leather trim for the instrument panel and upper doors and leather-accented steering wheel and gear selector.

Its front-wheel-drive PHEV system combines a 2.5-litre four-cylinder petrol engine with an electric motor for a combined 201kW output.

A 22.7kWh lithium-ion battery provides a claimed electric-only range of 121km on the WLTP test cycle. The existing front-wheel-drive RAV4 PHEV also supports 50kW DC charging and 11kW three-phase AC charging, giving it the ability to replenish its battery at public fast chargers as well as at home.

The GXL’s arrival will broaden Toyota’s plug-in offering as the RAV4 attempts to close the gap to Australia’s biggest-selling vehicles.

Toyota previously identified the new-generation RAV4 as a potential outright sales leader, raising the prospect of an SUV and electrified vehicle topping the annual Australian charts for the first time.

However, through August the RAV4 was fourth overall with 26,585 deliveries, behind the Ford Ranger on 32,796, Toyota HiLux on 32,161 and Tesla Model Y on 31,454.

That left the RAV4 6211 sales behind the Ranger with four months remaining — requiring it to average about 1553 more deliveries per month than the Ford to draw level.

Its August result was stronger: 5470 deliveries placed it second overall behind the Model Y’s 6414, ahead of the HiLux on 4833 and Ranger on 2440. Tesla reports separately from VFACTS, so its figures must be included when assessing the outright sales race.

The post Cheaper Toyota RAV4 PHEV confirmed for 2027: New GXL will bring price closer to Chinese SUV rivals appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Three-star setback: BYD Sealion 5 breaks brand’s perfect ANCAP run as M9 people-mover scores five
data.description:
The BYD Sealion 5 plug-in hybrid SUV has been awarded three ANCAP safety stars, ending the Chinese brand’s run of maximum five-star ratings.

The result contrasts with the five stars achieved by BYD’s new M9 plug-in hybrid people-mover, with both vehicles assessed locally against ANCAP’s tougher 2026–2028 protocols.

It will also not be welcome news for BYD because it is already dealing with a series of high profile issues.

The Sealion 5’s shortcomings were concentrated in crash avoidance and safe driving systems, although additional crash-protection assessments also revealed reduced protection for larger occupants and at higher crash severities.

READ MORE: BYD M9 lands from $61,990: Forget other Chinese people-movers, the M9 is aimed straight at the top-selling Kia Carnival
READ MORE: 2026 BYD Sealion 5 Essential Review: It’s Australia’s cheapest PHEV, so does that make it good value?
READ MORE: Cheap EVs clear tougher new ANCAP safety tests: Geely EX2 and Leapmotor B05 score five stars

The three-star rating covers both Essential and Premium versions of the five-seat SUV.

Until last week’s announcement of the smaller BYD Atto 2 DM-i, the Sealion 5 was Australia’s cheapest PHEV. It was also identified as a fleet opportunity at its launch earlier this year.

The result is likely to complicate that ambition, with five-star ANCAP ratings preferred by fleet buyers and required under many fleet purchasing policies.

ANCAP purchased six Sealion 5s for its assessment, while BYD supplied multiple M9s. Both programs involved right-hand-drive vehicles tested locally by ANCAP, rather than results drawn from its European counterpart Euro NCAP.

BYD had shown little enthusiasm for pursuing a Sealion 5 rating at launch, when there was already an expectation it would fall short of five stars.

ANCAP chief executive Carla Hoorweg confirmed the safety organisation independently selected the SUV for testing.

“Since then BYD has been, and continues to be, proactive in bringing forward models for ANCAP testing. However, the SEALION 5 was a model the brand hadn’t actively pursued for testing, and was subsequently selected by ANCAP to ensure consumers have a clear picture of its safety performance,” she said.

The Sealion 5 scored 48 per cent for Safe Driving, 51 per cent for Crash Avoidance, 79 per cent for Crash Protection and 74 per cent for Post-Crash performance. The M9 scored 75, 78, 89 and 100 per cent respectively.

The new protocols assess safety across those four stages, covering how a vehicle supports its driver, avoids collisions, protects people during a crash and assists occupants and emergency responders afterwards.

The Sealion 5 was new to Australia, but its origins are older. It is an updated version of the Chinese-market BYD Song Pro, which debuted in 2019.

That provides context for its safety specification, although ANCAP identified shortcomings in capabilities it has assessed for years, as well as newer requirements.

BYD’s previous five-star results were achieved under earlier protocols, which also imposed demanding requirements. The changed assessment structure means their individual category scores cannot be directly compared with these latest results.

BYD defended the Sealion 5, saying its rating reflected the strengthened testing requirements.

“The Sealion 5 is a safe vehicle that complies with all Australian Design Rules and regulatory safety standards,” a BYD spokesperson said.

“ANCAP introduced an updated testing protocol in 2026, with a strengthened assessment criteria compared to the 2023–2025 protocol which was applicable to the Sealion 5 at the time of its global introduction.

“The current rating reflects this new standard, not any change in BYD’s commitment to safety. Every other BYD vehicle tested by ANCAP has been awarded a five-star rating, which speaks to this commitment.”However, ANCAP stressed that the Sealion 5’s weaknesses extended beyond newly introduced requirements.

Its emergency lane-keeping system did not intervene when the vehicle departed towards the road edge, a capability ANCAP has encouraged since 2018.

Intervention to prevent collisions with oncoming or overtaking cars and motorcycles in an adjacent lane was also limited to speeds below 70km/h.

The SUV’s autonomous emergency braking system produced mixed results, with limitations in intersection scenarios, including T-bone collisions and turns across the path of pedestrians and cyclists.

Reverse autonomous emergency braking avoided collisions in only a limited number of assessed scenarios.

Child presence detection, which ANCAP has assessed since 2023, is not available. The Sealion 5 also lacks seatbelt misuse monitoring, occupant stature classification and a system to suppress unintended acceleration towards a pedestrian if the driver mistakenly presses the accelerator.

Its driver monitoring system could warn of several common forms of distraction but could not detect phone use or intervene for an unresponsive driver.

Physical crash testing produced stronger results, including maximum adult and child occupant-protection scores in the side-impact test.

However, the frontal offset test identified higher injury risks to the driver’s chest and lower legs and the front passenger’s neck. Structures within the dashboard were also identified as potential injury sources.

Additional sled and virtual assessments, which examine different occupant sizes and crash severities, revealed weaker protection than the conventional full-width frontal test.

ANCAP also applied a crash-compatibility deduction because the Sealion 5 presented a higher risk to occupants of an oncoming vehicle in a head-on collision.

A separate rollover-protection penalty was applied because BYD did not provide evidence demonstrating that the curtain airbags would deploy in a rollover and remain inflated for the required period.

The Sealion 5’s centre airbag performed effectively, and all child restraints selected for the installation assessment could be correctly installed in its rear seats.

Post-crash testing revealed another shortcoming: following the full-width frontal impact, battery voltage did not fall to the required level within the specified time, attracting a penalty.

Voltage isolation met requirements in the other three destructive crash tests, and battery thermal propagation performance scored full marks.

The Sealion 5 also lacks eCall, which can automatically summon assistance following a crash. Its seatbelt buckles, door releases and tailgate remained operable after the assessed impacts.

The M9 delivered stronger protection across frontal, side and rear-impact assessments, including maximum occupant-protection scores in the frontal offset and side-impact tests.

Its child presence detection system can notify the driver and activate the air-conditioning, while its lane departure prevention and low-speed collision avoidance systems performed well.

The people-mover achieved a perfect Post-Crash score, including effective battery voltage isolation, fire-risk management, accessible door releases and eCall.

However, its five-star result comes with qualifications. The rating currently covers seven-seat variants only, including Australia’s Premium. It does not cover the eight-seat Dynamic offered here. The vehicle tested was a seven-seat Dynamic variant sold in New Zealand.

ANCAP also identified marginal third-row whiplash protection. Most assessed child restraints could not be correctly installed in the third-row left seat, despite that position having ISOFIX and top-tether anchorages. Child restraints should not be used in the third-row centre or right seats.

Like the Sealion 5, the M9 attracted a crash-compatibility deduction because its structure presented a higher risk to occupants of an oncoming vehicle.

The post Three-star setback: BYD Sealion 5 breaks brand’s perfect ANCAP run as M9 people-mover scores five appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Range Rover Sport Electric priced for Australia: Two models starting from $226,518
data.description:
The first fully electric Range Rover Sport is available to order in Australia, priced from $226,518 plus on-road costs, with initial deliveries expected in March 2027.

The Range Rover Sport Electric comes in two grades: Dynamic HSE at $226,518 and Autobiography at $249,518, both before on-road costs. It joins the existing plug-in hybrid, petrol and diesel versions rather than replacing them.

The electric Sport enters a field of large luxury EV SUVs that includes the Porsche Cayenne Electric, Lotus Eletre and BMW iX.

READ MORE: Look out BMW iX5! Luxury Range Rover Sport to gain V8-beating all-electric power option
READ MORE: Range Rover Electric finally revealed: $317,718 luxury EV packs 405kW, 535km real-world range and 350kW charging
READ MORE: Wild Range Rover GT revealed: “Car-like” SUV-coupe EV arrives to fight electric versions of the BMW X6 and Mercedes GLE Coupe

The Cayenne S Electric is priced from $193,100 before on-road costs, below the entry Range Rover, while the Cayenne Turbo Electric sits above it at $259,900.

Both Sport electric grades use a 118.5kWh battery and two electric motors, one on each axle. Although each motor is rated at 260kW, their combined output is 404kW and 850Nm. Range Rover claims a 0–100km/h time of 4.5 seconds with Dynamic Launch engaged.

Claimed range is up to 600km on the NEDC test cycle. Range Rover also quotes a 535km estimate based on a production vehicle driven over a standardised route; actual results will depend on conditions and use.

The 800-volt electrical system supports a claimed 10–80 per cent DC charging time of about 22 minutes on a 350kW charger. Range Rover says 10 minutes at that charging rate can add up to 220km of NEDC range. A 22kW onboard AC charger is fitted.

The Sport Electric has more than a battery and motors separating it from its plug-in hybrid stablemate. Range Rover says its body structure is 61 per cent stiffer and its centre of gravity is 73mm lower.

Its chassis equipment includes air suspension, electronically controlled dampers, active roll control and all-wheel steering.

Range Rover also claims a 900mm wading depth and a 2500kg maximum braked towing capacity.

Those figures give the electric model capabilities that may matter to buyers considering it in place of a combustion-engined Sport, although towing and off-road use will affect driving range.

Exterior changes are relatively restrained, with an aerodynamically optimised grille and wheel designs among the identifying features.

The Sport Electric will be built at Solihull in the UK alongside the other Range Rover Sport variants, using batteries and motors produced at JLR’s Wolverhampton facility.

Inside, a 13.1-inch curved touchscreen runs the Pivi Pro infotainment system, accompanied by a 13.7-inch digital instrument display.

Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are standard, along with a 15W wireless phone charger. The system includes EV-specific controls for charging schedules and the powered charge-port door.

Range Rover lists available 22-way adjustable heated and ventilated front seats with massage, plus heated and ventilated reclining rear seats.

Buyers can also specify a Comfort Pack with four-zone climate control, a front console refrigerator, laminated side glass and cabin air purification.

The press material does not set out which of these items are standard on each Australian grade.

The battery carries an eight-year warranty, although Range Rover’s Australian material does not specify the local distance limit.

The post Range Rover Sport Electric priced for Australia: Two models starting from $226,518 appeared first on EV Central.
